steps.prompt: Before any explanation: which piece did your eye go to first in that position, and which one did you look at last?

steps.text: A **discovered attack** needs three pieces on one line. A *front piece* stands in the way. Behind it stands a *back piece*: a rook, bishop or queen. At the far end is a *target*. When the front piece moves away, the back piece suddenly attacks the target. Because the front piece also moves, one move can make two threats at once, and the opponent has only one move to answer both.

steps.text: The moving piece needs a job of its own. If it only steps aside, the opponent calmly saves the target. Its job can be a **check**, a **capture**, or a **threat against something bigger**. A check is the strongest, because the king must be rescued first. The front piece may even be lost on the way, as long as the back piece wins more than the front piece costs.

line.say: The bishop takes a bishop, and the black queen suddenly attacks the white queen.
White takes back, which wastes the move: the white queen is still attacked. Trading queens on a6 instead also leaves White a piece down [V, depth 16].
The queen takes the queen. The capture on e3 was the front piece's job.

steps.text: **Why it works.** You move one piece at a time, so a discovery sets two problems and allows one reply. After a check the opponent may move the king, block, or take the checking piece. Taking the front piece often answers the check, as in the boards above, but it does not stop the back piece hitting the target. [S] Nimzowitsch (*My System*, as summarised in our notes; we have not read the book) saw the hiding piece as nearly free. His wording is looser than the boards.

steps.title: Bishop and rook on the e-file
steps.prompt: Predict first. In the second position Black's king stands on h8. In the third the rook stands on d1.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight stands in front of the rook, and the black king stands on the same file.

line.say: The knight leaves the file: the rook now gives check, and the knight itself attacks the rook on h8.
Black blocks with the knight. A pawn cannot take the knight on g6, because that would not end the check.
The knight takes the rook. Two threats, one move.

claims.statement: Ng6+ wins material along the engine's line.
Before the move, no white piece attacks the rook on h8.
From g6 the knight attacks the rook on h8.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop on e4 hides the rook on e1 from the queen on e8, and the black king stands on g8.

line.say: The bishop captures with check on the king, and uncovers the rook's attack on the queen.
Black takes the bishop, which answers the check. The engine's best reply is actually the king stepping to f8, but Black still loses the queen for a rook [V, depth 16].
The rook takes the queen.

claims.statement: Bxh7+ wins material along the engine's line.
Before the bishop moves, the bishop blocks the rook's attack on e8.
After the bishop leaves e4, the rook attacks the queen on e8.

steps.caption: Now move the king to h8. The bishop can still capture on h7, but the capture is no longer check. The contrast is about this one capture.

line.say: The bishop takes a pawn. It attacks nothing and gives no check.
The bishop was shielding the rook from the queen. Now the queen takes the rook and it is mate on the back rank.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates Bxh7 at least 300 centipawns below the best move.
Before the bishop moves, the bishop blocks the black queen's line to e1.
After the bishop leaves e4, the black queen attacks the rook on e1.

steps.caption: Back to the king on g8, but the rook now stands on d1. The check is there; the line to the queen is not.

line.say: The bishop captures with check, as before.
Black takes it. The rook on d1 attacks nothing new, so White has just lost a bishop for a pawn.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates Bxh7+ at least 100 centipawns below the best move.
After the bishop moves, nothing of White's attacks the queen on e8.

steps.text: **What the opponent can try.** After a discovery the defender has a few ideas: take the front piece, block the line, move or defend the target, or check first. A double check, where front and back piece both give check, leaves only a king move. [I] This list is our working summary, not a standard. Boards for blocking and for a defended target are not yet in this lesson.

**Three questions before you trust one** ([I] our working checklist, not a standard). Is there a clear line from the back piece to something worth winning? Does the front piece move with a check, a capture or a bigger threat? Can the opponent hit the back piece with tempo, or is it undefended, so the trade stops being good for you? If all three answers are good, look closer. It is a rule of thumb: always find the opponent's best answer.

steps.prompt: Pick one defence from the list and say how you would set it up on a board, so you can test whether the discovery still works.

steps.text: [H] **Why are these missed?** A guess, not tested: the eye follows the piece that is about to move. A back piece looks idle until the front piece leaves, so it does not feel like an attacker. If so, the cure is to look along every line a slider stands on as if the piece in front were gone. [I] Nimzowitsch's remark about the hiding piece fits this, but he gave no data.

steps.chapter: Set it up or stop it

steps.text: **Building a discovery.** Put a slider on a line, put your own piece in front of it, and aim the line at something that matters: a king, a queen, a loose piece. Now the front piece can move whenever it has a good move, and the opponent must keep watching that line. [H] Such a battery may be worth more as a standing threat than as a quick strike; I have not measured this.

steps.caption: Prevention first. Black to move in a game with the queens on the same rank and a white bishop between them. Castling looks natural.

The bishop takes h7 with check and uncovers the white queen's attack on the black queen.

steps.text: **Stopping one.** Before you move, scan the lines through your king and queen. Is an enemy slider aiming along one, with his own piece in front? Ask what that piece could do next, and pick a move that survives: move the target, block the line, or remove the back piece. Castling on autopilot and grabbing a pawn are the usual ways in. Several of the next boards come from Lichess puzzle data (CC0); the earliest in this lesson are constructed.

No labels from here. About one Lichess puzzle in twenty carries the discovered-attack theme (311,174 of 6,157,341, our count from the CC0 file) [V]. Puzzles are chosen because they hold a tactic, so this is not how often you will meet one in your own games [I]. Expect positions where nothing is hidden, and where the right answer is that there is no tactic.

A game between two strong players: Negi (White, rated 2671) against Richter (Black, 2473), Bundesliga 2013-14, round 14, 5 April 2014, drawn [V, TWIC record in our data]. White has set a battery on the f-file. Watch how a sacrifice drags the black king in front of it.

steps.text: The discovery did not win the game. The engine (depth 16) rated the position slightly worse for White before it and close to level after [V]. A discovery can regain material or save a game as well as win one.

**Check yourself.** Can you name the three pieces, and say what job the front piece needs? Can you say when it fails: the line is shut, the front piece has no job, or the opponent takes the back piece first? Remember to scan every line from a back piece.

steps.text: **One model answer.** Set up the position of the third demonstration: front piece the bishop on e4, back piece the rook on e1, target the queen on e8. The bishop captures on h7 with check, so Black must answer the check before saving the queen. It fails if the king stands on h8 (no check) or the rook stands on d1 (no line). The usual mistake is to look only at the piece that moves.
